national.title: What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
national.summary: Six people were killed in a random shooting in Krakow's main square, and three bodies were later found at the home of the attacker.
national.body:
At least six people were killed and more than a dozen others injured when a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland.

Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here is everything we know so far.

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city which is popular with tourists.

Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".

Footage shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.

A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

A 25-year-old man who was arrested remains in hospital after having surgery for a gunshot wound. The Krakow branch of the National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland has announced an investigation into what constitutes "a terrorist offence".

national.title: More than 600,000 left with no power in Ukraine after strikes, authorities say
national.summary: Ukraine has been bracing for Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
national.body: Hundreds of thousands of people were left without power after Russian strikes hit Ukraine's energy infrastructure, authorities said on Sunday.In the central Dnipropetrovsk region, "more than 600,000 residents of the region have been left without power," power company DTEK said on Telegram after a "night attack has damaged important energy facilities".It said the company was working to restore electricity but the task was "complicated by repeated attacks".Ukrainian President Volodymyr previously accused Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of trilateral talks next week with Russia.In another strike, a Russian drone hit "a critical infrastructure facility" in the northeastern Kharkiv region, the mayor of Zlatopil city, Mykola Baksheyev, said on social media."Nearly 250,000 customers in the Kharkiv region were left without power," Baksheyev said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the night-time strikes had triggered "widespread power outages across the country"."In the Zhytomyr region alone, 140 apartment buildings were left without heating following a Russian strike," he said, as temperatures in Ukraine already hovered around freezing.He also said Russia had launched a drone at Komyshuvakha, a village in the Zaporizhzhia region where Moscow had hit an aid distribution centre on Monday in one of the deadliest attacks of the war.The death toll has risen to 55 people, Zelenskyy said. Emergency services previously put it at 50 killed."This morning, the Russians attacked Komyshuvakha with an FPV drone, where emergency rescue operations have been underway for seven days ... Unfortunately, more people may still be under the rubble," Zelenskyy said.The strikes came a day after Ukraine's energy ministry said a massive attack on energy facilities had plunged residents in five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv.

national.title: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
national.summary: El Niño rains have transformed Chile's Atacama Desert into a spectacular sea of color, awakening a fleeting ecosystem of flowers and wildlife in one of the driest places on Earth.
national.body:
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption

COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.

This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.

Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.

A field of wildflowers blooms across Chile's Atacama Desert during the rare flowering phenomenon known as Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom, triggered by unusually heavy rainfall that awakens dormant seeds. The brief blooms transform the world's driest nonpolar desert into a landscape of pink, purple, yellow and white. Huasco, Chile, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption

But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.

The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.

national.title: How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
national.summary: Video authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment gunshots rang out in Krakow's main market square.
national.body:
How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded Close Six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second largest city, on Saturday.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows about a dozen people running inside two buildings before a black car with its front window open passes, followed by a police car.

Another video shows the moment that gunshots were heard in the city's main market square.

Poland's interior minister described the suspect - a 25-year-old Polish citizen - as being inspired by "far-right ideologies"; police said he used "military weapons" in the attack.

Hours after the attack, Polish PM Donald Tusk said three other bodies were found at the suspect's home, which is still being searched.

national.title: Italy's leader blames pro-Russian hackers for personal data leaks
national.summary: Italy's foreign minister said he was targeted because of his country's support for Ukraine.
national.body: Italy's prime minister blamed pro-Russian hackers for leaking the country's foreign minister's data onto the dark web.Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday he has been subjected to intimidation and that his personal data was leaked because of his support for Ukraine, but did not specify who was behind it.In a post on X, Tajani blamed "cybercriminals" for posting his personal data on the dark web, a term used to describe a section of the internet only accessible with specialist software, commonly associated with criminal activities.In a separate statement on Saturday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed "pro-Russian hackers" for the leaks. Meloni expressed her "full solidarity" with the foreign minister over "what has come to light regarding the activities of pro-Russian hackers and the dissemination of personal data relating to him on the dark web.""The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," Meloni added.Tajani said the leaks have been going for days and expose him to threats and intimidation. He added that his family have also been targeted and the perpetrators are still looking for more information."Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," the minister said. "Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous for these criminal entities."Tajani said he would not be intimidated by the incident and vowed to continue his support of Italian allies."I will continue working to defend my ministry and Italy, and I will keep strengthening ties and cooperation with our allies so that we can protect ourselves together," the minister said.

national.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
national.summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White.
national.body:
FILE - President Donald Trump waves alongside Dana White, president and CEO of UFC, as they arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House, June 14, 2026, in Washington. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

Sports UFC boss Dana White says 'never again' to another White House fight night White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

national.summary: A New York City Department of Education employee is facing a murder charge in the stabbing death of a 28-year-old woman last week in Brooklyn, authorities announced Saturday.
national.body: A New York City Department of Education employee is facing a murder charge in the stabbing death of a 28-year-old woman last week in Brooklyn, authorities announced Saturday. Katie Suarez was stabbed while jogging along the Shore Parkway greenway in Brooklyn on the evening of Oct. 30. Her father found Suarez injured along the path. She was rushed to the hospital with a stab wound to her neck but ultimately died from her injuries. On Saturday, the NYPD said it had arrested 27-year-old Sayed Mohassib, of Bath Beach, Brooklyn. Mohassib is charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence, and criminal possession of a weapon. Mohassib, wearing flip flops and a red jacket, did not answer any questions when police walked him out of the 62nd Precinct Saturday afternoon. The circumstances leading to Suarez's killing were not immediately clear. It also wasn't immediately clear what led police to Mohassib. NYPD sources say he made statements claiming he "blacked out" and doesn't remember hurting anyone. Mohassib was taken in for questioning Friday, police sources said, but they have not yet shared details on how they tied him to the crime. Police sources say Mohassib and Suarez both attended Brooklyn College at the same time, but right now there's no evidence that they knew each other. The suspect is an employee of the New York City Department of Education. Police sources say he worked at Public School 200 in Brooklyn, and that he was also a member of the NYPD in field training in the Bronx from October to November 2022. Elected officials said he was employed as a teacher's aide and police sources say he was on the job at PS 200 near the precinct this past week. "The safety of our students is our very top priority. We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction. national.title: Houthis say at least 33 killed in Saudi air strike
national.summary: Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, has not commented.
national.body:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 33 people, including women and children, have been killed in air strikes by Saudi Arabia.

There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.

The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.

Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia on Saturday. It added that 39 people had been injured.

The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.

national.title: 1 dead, at least a dozen hurt after car strikes cyclists in North Carolina
national.summary: One person was killed and at least a dozen others injured when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said.
national.body: One person was killed and several others injured Saturday morning when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said. According to North Carolina State Highway Patrol, a little after 9:30 a.m. Eastern time a black Infiniti passenger car was traveling west on a road in Wake County when it crossed the center line and crashed into a group of cyclists who were biking east. The driver did not stop at the scene, but continued for about a half-mile before crashing into a ditch on the side of the road, state highway patrol said. Holly Springs Fire Chief LeRoy Smith said seven people were transported to a hospital with major injuries and 15 others sustained minor injuries. State highway patrol pegged the injury toll at about a dozen, however. The deceased victim was identified by state highway patrol as 63-year-old Patrick Allen Turner of Cary, North Carolina. The suspected driver, 76-year-old Donald Robert Morris-Jones of Apex, North Carolina, was arrested on multiple charges, including felony death by vehicle, felony serious injury by vehicle, felony hit-and-run involving serious injury or death, reckless driving and driving while impaired, according to officials. He is being held on $1 million bond. People at the scene told Smith the cyclists were part of a group that regularly gathers for weekend bike rides.Wake County is located about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.

national.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
national.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.
national.body:
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.

The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.

But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.

The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.

The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.

It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

national.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
national.summary: While some believe the site should be partially or completely rebuilt, others want it abandoned and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
national.body:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

national.title: 'Dana, please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss to be White House press secretary
national.summary: It was unclear how genuine the president's offer was, although White later said he would travel to Washington for them to meet.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post.

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"

It was unclear whether the president's public job offer was genuine, although White said later on Saturday: "I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday".

The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days into the job.

Trump's post on Saturday afternoon comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.

The president called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country".

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters.

Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room.

national.title: Democrats win Senate control — live updates
national.summary: Democrats were able to pick up the seats needed to gain control of the Senate, CBS News projects, and the party scored several upset victories in red states.
national.body: Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland urged his Democratic colleagues to show restraint in the selection process of their Senate majority leader in the wake of the party's dominant showing in the midterm elections this week. "There should be no coronation," Van Hollen said during an interview Saturday at the Crooked Con political conference in Washington, D.C. "I said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic Caucus. We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers, and that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we're going to go." The Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the upper chamber when the new session of Congress convenes in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic Caucus since 2017, but several incoming Democratic Senators-elect have signaled they want to see new leadership. "This is why I said it's really important that people withhold any commitments on the Senate leadership races until we have a chance to hear from our new members who just got off the campaign trail and have been directly in touch with voters," Van Hollen said. national.title: Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
national.summary: Homelessness declined after years of record-high levels but it still remains at nearly 700,000. The Trump administration and homeless advocacy groups cite different reasons for the drop.
national.body:
People line up along temporary tents to partake in a free Thanksgiving meal provided by the Union Rescue Mission as the Los Angeles Skid Row district annual feast hosts thousands of homeless and others in need, in downtown Los Angeles on Nov. 24, 2022. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption

After years of increasing to record-high levels , the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.

"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Only on NPR A homeless man was charged with a felony for camping. He's one of the first The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options , housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.

Chris Van Hollen of Maryland urged his Democratic colleagues to show restraint in the selection process of their Senate majority leader in the wake of the party's dominant showing in the midterm elections this week. We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers, and that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we're going to go." national.title: What is Diwali, the Festival of Lights, and how is it celebrated?
national.summary: The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8.
national.body:
Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Deepa Bharath, Associated Press

Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and widely marked by prayers, family gatherings and the lighting of fireworks.

More than one billion people across faiths celebrate it in the world's most populous nation and its diaspora.

The name Diwali comes from "Deepavali," meaning "a row of lights." Celebrants place rows of traditional clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance.

The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8.

While Diwali is a major religious festival for Hindus, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Its origin stories vary by region but share a theme: the victory of good over evil.

In southern India, Diwali celebrates Lord Krishna's victory over the demon Naraka, who is said to have imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. In northern India, it honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife, Sita, and his brother, Lakshmana, after 14 years of exile in the forest.

national.title: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
national.summary: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election.
national.body:
Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.

Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.

Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.

"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.

No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.

Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.

national.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
national.summary: The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls.
national.body:
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.

"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."

"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.

"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.

But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.

More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.

A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.

national.summary: Researchers found that the stroke incidence rate among adults from 1993-94 nearly doubled in 2020, jumping from 33.90 cases per 100,000 people to 62.18 cases.
national.body:
After U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, a 53-year-old Democrat representing Connecticut, was hospitalized Oct. 31 following a stroke, his chief of staff said she was "optimistic" he will make a full recovery.

Stroke rates are higher overall among older adults, so a stroke at his age may sound surprising — but it's become more common.

WATCH: Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke

Stroke rates among adults ages 20 to 54 years old have risen in the last 30 years. Researchers found that the stroke incidence rate among adults from 1993-94 nearly doubled in 2020, jumping from 33.90 cases per 100,000 people to 62.18 cases. Stroke rates remain much higher overall among older adults, but the rate for older people declined during the same period.

When Centers for Disease Control and Prevention researchers compared stroke incidence data from 2011-13 with 2020-22, they found that stroke prevalence increased 14.6% among people 18 to 44 and 15.7% among people 45 to 64.

There isn't one single explanation for the rise, but risk factors for stroke such as high blood pressure and obesity are up among young people, too.

A study in Florida found that from 2014 to 2022, young patients (18 to 55 years old) who experienced the most common form of stroke increasingly had existing vascular risk factors such as hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes or sleep apnea.

To decrease stroke risk, health professionals advise people to quit smoking and using drugs recreationally and to eat a balanced diet that incorporates many colorful fruits and vegetables. It's important to maintain an active lifestyle and manage conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes and cholesterol.

national.summary: Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a clear majority in the vote. But in marathon discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.
national.body:
Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press

JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.

Eisenkot, a former military chief who ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is now a step closer to ousting Israel's longest-serving premier.

"This is the time to establish a national emergency government. I will do anything possible to prove us worthy," Eisenkot posted on his X account just after the presidential announcement.

He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond.

In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government. But putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught and any possible coalition would require candidates to make tough compromises that could outrage their own voters.

Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority in parliament in last month's elections. But the bloc led by Eisenkot also didn't win a majority. That left Arab-led parties, which made historic gains, as potential but politically fraught kingmakers.

An Arab party has been part of a governing coalition just once in Israel's history. Forming such an alliance could be especially divisive for Eisenkot after more than three years of war in Gaza.

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage last month in Tel Aviv following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption

Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.

President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday. Herzog made the decision after parties representing most of the members of Israel's parliament recommended Eisenkot to try forming a governing coalition.

Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages.

Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.

He leads the center-right Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.

That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Melania Trump on Saturday announced a multimillion dollar partnership between Louisiana State University and her "Fostering the Future" program to provide scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system.

"This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation and a chance to build a wonderful life," she said at an event with LSU President Wade Rousse.

MMR Group Inc., an electrical contracting company based in Baton Rouge, committed $5 million, with additional LSU Foundation donors providing more than $2 million, the White House said.

The first lady later planned to attend the football game between LSU and Alabama, which also is participating in the initiative.

"As adults, we have a moral obligation to our children, especially those in foster care. But, as you know, we must act to truly make a difference. The foster care community doesn't need words," she added, before concluding her brief remarks by saying, "Now, let's go and enjoy the game."

national.title: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
national.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.
national.body:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.

He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

national.title: Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say
national.summary: A gunman targeted random people as he drove into Krakow's Main Square, a major tourist spot. Police shot and wounded the gunman during a gunfight.
national.body:
Police cars are parked in a cordoned off area after a shooter opened fire in a market square in Krakow, Poland, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, Beata Zawrzel/AP hide caption

KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.

The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow's Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.

The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn't release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.

Four women and two men were killed in the Krakow attack. At least three of the women were Polish, and one of the dead was a U.K. citizen, authorities said. Police were still trying to identify the other two people who were killed.

national.title: Judge wants former U.S. attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
national.summary: The administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events."
national.body:
Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.

Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.

The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" of the course while the lawsuit is active.

Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.

Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.

As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job.

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV urged Uruguayans on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, as he delivered an ode to the region's beloved mate tea and raised the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country.

After arriving Friday, Leo spent his first full day in Uruguay pointing to the church's historic roots in the country and the work it's doing today. He visited a Catholic university and a violence-ravaged neighborhood of Montevideo where church groups have built homes, provided job opportunities and run drug rehabilitation programs.

The aim, on the first stop of his three-nation South American tour, is to propose the Catholic faith as a response to today's challenges and the church a willing helper in a country where even Catholic holidays have secular names and God cannot be mentioned in oaths of office.

Leo traveled first to Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina, for his first Mass in South America. The Vatican said 40,000 people -- many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil – came out, despite the morning rain and blustery gray skies.

The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of "Olé, olé, olé, olé, pope, pope!" when Leo's plane landed in Paysandú, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in a park.

The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.

The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.

President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated " following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.

Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.

Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.

The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.

As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.

Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.

national.title: Scott Colom and Black Mississippians stand on the cusp of Senate history as vote count stretches on
national.summary: The state is still tallying ballots that could make Colom the first Black senator from this Deep South state since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
national.body:
Sophie Bates, Associated Press Sophie Bates, Associated Press

JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democrat Scott Colom hasn't won Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, but the local prosecutor was welcomed as a historic figure Friday as he strolled through the Farish Street business district where civil rights leaders once organized.

"It's so wonderful! It's so wonderful to have Scott Colom as our representative," said Maati Jone Primm, who owns Marshall's Music & Bookstore in Jackson.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The state is still tallying ballots that could make Colom the first Black senator from this Deep South state since post-Civil War Reconstruction. The possibility of Colom defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith puts many Black voters somewhere between cautious optimism and outright celebration in a state where nearly 40% of the population is Black but the top representation for generations has been white.

"I'm so glad we are at the point where we are," said Sorie Tarawally, a 76-year-old attorney who has long known Colom's father. He called the 43-year-old candidate "the man, our messiah, our savior."

The contest remains too early for The Associated Press to call, and Colom's historic bid will hinge on a tedious process playing out in elections offices across Mississippi's 82 counties. Local officials are receiving and examining absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots, before deadlines next week. Volunteers and lawyers representing each campaign look on in anticipation of potential litigation.

"We're going to make sure everything is followed according to the law, and I have confidence in those local officials," Colom said. "They're doing their jobs. Got to be patient with them."

Moriah Balingit, Associated Press Moriah Balingit, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is behind many of the administration's signature domestic policy initiatives — especially its sweeping crackdown on immigration.

An outspoken defender of Trump's most far-reaching goals to remake government going back to his 2016 run for president, Miller is known for his harsh language and unapologetic bombast, attracting outsized attention from supporters and critics alike. His record is likely to be scrutinized by Democrats in his powerful new role as he leads Trump's White House through a difficult lame duck period after the Republican Party lost both houses of Congress.

Here are some memorable things Miller has said through the years:

During a 2023 spike in illegal border crossings, Miller described migrants as invaders, even though many were escaping poverty and violence in their home countries.

"We are being conquered," he told Fox News Channel in December 2023, commenting on the sharp rise. "We have millions of people coming in from different cultures and different ways of living and different belief systems."

Miller also warned that "a generation from now," people "will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there's massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable."

national.title: Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing 6 people and wounding 16
national.summary: The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, opened fire with an automatic weapon in the city's Main Square. He was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical views," Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said at a news conference.
national.body:
Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press

Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press

Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press

KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.

The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow's Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.

The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn't release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

national.title: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
national.summary: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was removed from office and placed under house arrest Friday. The Senate voted on his impeachment after the collapse of a state-affiliated bank.
national.body:
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money.

Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population.

He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.

Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.

World, reordering Brazil's left-wing President Lula elected for fourth term A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning . The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012.

Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation . Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process.

At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website .

Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest .

local.body:
I heard it as a teenager. I said it as a parent and a teacher. You may have too. "How can you listen to that crap? It's terrible. Do you even know what the lyrics are saying? That's not music." And you may have given or received the same response. "I don't listen to the words. I just like the beat." Or something to the effect of, "The artist is just expressing their emotions or making social commentary." Or " I don't mind the profanity, that's just the way that they talk."

I never actively looked for Christian-themed music until I taught my son's Faith Formation class more than a decade ago. There were Christian songs that I enjoyed listening to after stumbling upon them as a boy, teenager or adult. Some of these songs I didn't even know were Christian themed until I closely examined the lyrics. "Kyrie" by Mister Mister is a perfect example. I am not sure that George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord" is truly Christian themed but I do remember thoroughly enjoying listening to Harrison's song being sung during mass at St. Anthony's in the early 70s. You have to be of a certain age to remember Sister Janet Mead's 1974 hit "The Lord's Prayer" or Norman Greenbaum's 1969 hit "Spirit in the Sky". I don't remember there being Christian radio stations when I was growing up but I was never pointed in that direction. I listened exclusively to Top 40 music when I was a kid and a young adult except when forced to listen to other styles of music.

I volunteered to teach my son's Faith Formation class because St. Anthony's could not find an instructor at the time. I soon found out that teaching Catholic Doctrine and the Christian Faith was a bit more difficult than teaching mathematics to kids. While it was challenging teaching Faith Formation, it was also very rewarding. Just like teaching mathematics, I have learned so much about Catholicism and my Christian faith by studying it in order to teach it to others.

One of the ways that I tried to engage youngsters learning about Jesus was through music. I had upbeat Christian music playing for my Sunday School students as they entered the classroom each week. I pointed out to them that no matter what genre of music you like, there are artists performing Christian songs in that genre. There is Christian Rock, Christian Rap, Christian Heavy Metal, Christian Pop and Christian Country music. I told my Sunday School students, if you like a certain style of music, find a Christian artist that performs it, listen and enjoy it. And if you're really not concerned with the lyrics then why not listen to a style of music that doesn't include messages about sex, violence, drugs and other vices? A positive message just might come to you as you enjoy the rhythm and the beat of your favorite style of music with a Christian theme.

local.body:
The operators of a veterans retreat in Bemus Point are fighting charges filed in August by the state Attorney General’s Office.

Attorney General Letitia James alleges Healing for Heroes – A Disabled Veteran’s Retreat and Wooded Oasis Inc. defrauded donors, billed itself as an outdoor retreat for disabled veterans and hosted limited retreats that served board members and their friends and family - essentially using the charity to fund their own vacations. An investigation by the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) found that the owners of Healing for Heroes’ 30-acre property, Board President Thomas Nelsen and Jennifer Milchanoski-Nelsen, board secretary and treasurer, rented out the property on Airbnb on at least 32 different occasions in 2024 and 2025, claiming all proceeds would go to their charity. Instead, the couple kept the $33,312.16 proceeds from the rentals for themselves. The Attorney General’s office investigation also found that almost half of the nearly $100,000 donated to the organization was spent on property maintenance and improvements, such as a bathroom renovation and a new deck for the property, as well as personal shopping, meals, vehicle repair and gas expenses for board members.

The Nelsens, through their attorney, are fighting back in court documents filed recently in state Supreme Court in Erie County.

“This case is a classic example of government overreach,” attorney Ryan K. Cummings of Hodgson Russ LLP in Buffalo wrote in his Memorandum in Opposition to the state’s petition. “The Attorney General’s office began with the headline it wanted for its election-season press release and created a story to support that headline. The AG’s story is a fiction based on assumptions, innuendo, and falsehoods. As a threshold matter, the petition is not supported by evidence in admissible form. It is built on attorney representations that are not made on personal knowledge. It relies on a series of documents that have not been authenticated or provided and in many instances those summaries are demonstrably wrong. Finally, the petition is predicated on two affirmations from the fall of 2025 by two individuals who were tangentially involved with Healing for Heroes – A Disabled Veteran’s Retreat and Wooded Oasis Inc., separated from the organization in May 2024 and February 2025, respectively, and who were unceremoniously cut off from the organization following dishonorable conduct. The AG’s house of cards collapses under the weight of these infirmities.”

local.title: Club hears history of artist Norman Rockwell
local.summary: Joyce Haines presented her paper on notable New Yorker, Norman Rockwell, at a recent meeting of the Fredonia Shakespeare Club, hosted by Ms. Lucille Richardson. Although Norman Perceval Rockwell was born in New York City in 1884, making him a Notable New Yorker, he moved to Vermont and later to Stoc
local.body:
Joyce Haines presented her paper on notable New Yorker, Norman Rockwell, at a recent meeting of the Fredonia Shakespeare Club, hosted by Ms. Lucille Richardson.

Although Norman Perceval Rockwell was born in New York City in 1884, making him a Notable New Yorker, he moved to Vermont and later to Stockbridge, Mass., where he delighted in a calm, idyllic location to work on his paintings and illustrations.

Rockwell loved to tell stories in pictures. He always considered the concept, clothes, props, postures, and profiles of his subject, then photographed them, made sketches, and produced the illustration. He used local people for his models. Haines showed an original cover from The Saturday Evening Post, published the month and year she was born, which was the cover of her baby book written by her mother.

In 1941 wartime, President Franklin D. Roosevelt gave a speech about the four freedoms of Americans to inspire everyone. Rockwell wanted to do something for the war effort, so he did paintings representing each of the four freedoms in 1943: Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, Freedom from Want and Freedom from Fear. Signed prints were distributed in schools and libraries, and those raised over $130 billion in bonds at rallies for the war effort.

In the 1960s, Rockwell turned to something more serious, working on the painting Do unto Others as You Would Have Them Do unto You. Members viewed a short video narrated by Rockwell himself detailing the making of this painting.

In 1963, he left the Post, and began making covers for Look magazine, where he had more freedom without constraints. It was a time of civil rights and desegregation. He expressed his thoughts with his painting of The Problem We All Live With, a depiction of Ruby Bridges being accompanied by guards on her first day of attending a white school.

Rockwell, a heavy smoker, died on Nov. 8, 1978, of emphysema at the age of 84 in his Stockbridge home.

A pristine museum located on the grounds of a well-groomed 36-acre campus just outside the village of Stockbridge houses his legacy of an archive of reference photographs, business and fan correspondence, props, costumes, and other materials that reflect his personal and professional life. It is just of the border from New York State off the I-90 and is well worth a visit.

JAMESTOWN - Audubon Community Nature Center has two fun learning opportunities for kids happening soon.

November Camp is Wednesday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m., with reservations required by Monday at AudubonCNC.org/november-camp. Ages 4-12 can enjoy the school holiday outdoors, being active before the cold sets in. They can explore, play, climb, run, and learn about animals gathering and storing food and plants ready to spend the winter in a state of dormancy. Learning and play are the themes of the day! Children should dress for the weather, bring water, snacks, lunch, and extras of anything that might get wet. Three- to 8-year-olds and their favorite grown-ups will learn about "Fur, Feathers, and Scales," the different coverings on animals' bodies to help them survive. Explore and compare these and learn how each adaptation helps the animals find food and survive predators or the climate. Enjoy a nature lesson, walk, and craft if there is time. The fee is $12 adults, $9 Nature Center members and children ages 3-8.

Audubon Community Nature Center is located at 1600 Riverside Road, one-quarter mile east of Route 62 between Jamestown, N.Y., and Warren, Pa. You can visit the nearly 600-acre nature preserve, look in on the live birds of prey, enjoy the native tree arboretum and Nature Play Area, and hike the six miles of trails dawn until dusk daily for free.

The three-story Nature Center building houses interactive displays, live animals, the Ralph Simpson Bird Collection, the indoor Nature Play Area, and the Blue Heron Gift Shop. Visitors are welcome Mondays through Saturdays, 10 a.m.-4:30 p.m., and Sundays, 1-4:30 p.m. Nature Center members and SNAP/EBT and Arts Access cardholders have free building admission daily. Audubon Community Nature Center builds and nurtures connections between people and nature by providing positive outdoor experiences, opportunities to learn about and understand the natural world, and knowledge to act in environmentally responsible ways.

Special connection always on display at Centaur Stride
local.summary: The bond between horse and human is built on trust, recognition, and a quiet kind of love. What makes an animal a service or therapy animal? Is it the training, the loyalty, the connection, or perhaps the special garments, paperwork, and fees that sometimes accompany that designation? While these th
local.body:
Horses and humans have a special connection at Centaur Stride.

The bond between horse and human is built on trust, recognition, and a quiet kind of love.

What makes an animal a service or therapy animal? Is it the training, the loyalty, the connection, or perhaps the special garments, paperwork, and fees that sometimes accompany that designation? While these things may define an animal’s role, they don’t necessarily explain what makes the relationship between an animal and a human so extraordinary.

From the cherished stuffed animal of childhood to the faithful companion who walks beside us later in life, animals offer comfort, companionship, reassurance, and something difficult to put into words: the feeling that we are not alone. When it comes to emotional well-being, the connection itself can speak louder than any certificate.

Anyone who has welcomed a dog home after an absence knows the excitement of that reunion. The wagging tail, dancing feet, and unmistakable joy remind us how deeply animals can recognize and value our presence. Similar reunions between people and animals raised in human care remind us that connection can endure even across time and distance.

Every human being needs to feel recognized, welcomed, valued, and loved. But what happens when a disability makes it difficult or impossible for someone to care for an animal independently? Can that person still experience the remarkable connection animals offer?

This is where therapy animals can make such a meaningful difference.

An animal’s ability to connect with someone doesn’t depend on being that person’s personal pet. Through appropriate training, compassionate handling, and consistent care, animals can develop trusting relationships with many different people. They become partners in shared experiences, offering encouragement, confidence, companionship, and a sense of accomplishment.

Can I find out everything about my family from online sources? Absolutely not. It’s estimated that only 10% of genealogical records are available online; the rest are in archives, courthouses, and libraries. Also, there’s nothing like researching ‘offline’. local.title: NIAGARA DISCOVERIES: Portraits at the Col. William Bond House
local.summary: It’s sometimes odd how one thing leads to another when doing historical research. Several years ago, this column highlighted a few stories about twins in Lockport in the 19th century. While rereading that article again for possible revision and expansion,…
local.body:
It’s sometimes odd how one thing leads to another when doing historical research. Several years ago, this column highlighted a few stories about twins in Lockport in the 19th century. While rereading that article again for possible revision and expansion, it led to thinking about the portrait of two young ladies in the parlor of the Col. William Bond House at 143 Ontario St. in Lockport. The girls are obviously sisters, and could even be taken as twins. Suggestions have been made to their identity, but it was never determined (as far as I know). Since the other portraits in the house are of prominent local people, it was thought that they were too. A Google image search found that this was far from the case.

The young ladies in the portrait are Russian Princesses Anna Petrovna (1777-1805) and Ekaterina Petrovna (1783-1830) Lopukhin. It is a painted copy of a watercolor, by an unknown artist. Though undated, the original is early 19th century and is in an art gallery in Moscow. It must have been a popular image to reproduce as there are many variations for sale online. Anna Petrovna Lopukhin was from the Russian nobility and at age 19, became the mistress of Emperor Paul I, son of Catherine the Great. This caused much court intrigue and three years later she left court and married her childhood sweetheart, Prince Paul Gagarin, in 1799. Tragically, she died of consumption in 1805 before her 28th birthday, leaving no children. Her sister, Ekaterina Petrovna Lopukhin, married Grigory Alexandrovich Demidov in 1797. She had two children and died in 1830 at the age of 47. Not much could be found on either of these ladies.

Ann Marie Linnabery is the assistant director of the History Center of Niagara.

local.body:
Bob Eadie’s stands for a photo in his Newfane barbershop prior to this retirement. He closed up shop on Oct. 30 after 67 years as a barber.

LEFT: One of the many honors displayed in Bob Eadie’s Barbershop. RIGHT: Bob Eadie made quite the impact on the community and his loyal customers over the years.

Bob Eadie made quite the impact on the community and his loyal customers over the years.

Bob Eadie put away his clippers for good on Friday, Oct. 30.

For generations of Newfane families, a trip to Bob Eadie’s Barbershop was about more than getting a haircut. It was a chance to catch up, share a story and spend time with a man who became part of the fabric of the community. After 67 years behind the chair, Eadie has retired, closing a chapter on a business and a hometown legacy built one haircut at a time.

Robert Eadie moved from Clearfield, Pennsylvania, to Newfane when he was 12. As a teenager looking to find his place in a new community, he was quickly drawn to attending many of the high school athletic games — football, basketball, and wrestling. He also found his foot in the door at Bill Murphy’s Barbershop, where his first job and opportunity in the barbering profession began as a cleaner. At about 16 years of age, Bill asked Bob if he would like an apprenticeship position at the shop. There were three other apprentices at that time. The apprenticeships were state-regulated and emphasized sanitation, clipper work, and razor techniques. Once he completed his apprenticeship, he became a partner with Mr. Murphy. After graduation, Bob married his high school sweetheart, Sheila, and by 1961 they welcomed their firstborn. At just 19 years old, he quickly learned perseverance and the meaning of hard work.

entertainment.summary: The 34th edition of Camerimage kicked off with Luca Guadagnino’s 'Artificial' and included honors for Darren Aronofsky and the THR Visionary Award for cinematographer Janusz Kamiński.
entertainment.body:
The AI elephant in the room took center stage on Saturday at the opening night of the 34th Camerimage Film Festival.

Instead of avoiding the divisive issue of artificial intelligence , the Polish fest, the world’s leading festival for the celebration of the art of cinematography, doubled down.

For the opening address, in place of festival director Marek Żydowicz, Camerimage sent a humanoid robot, called “Edward Warchocki,” on stage. The slightly tottering, Polish-speaking android addressed the crowd before Żydowicz joined it for an extended back-and-forth about the role of AI in cinema. The “hopes and threats” of the technology, Żydowicz stressed , would be a major talking point throughout the seven-day event in Toruń. Related Stories Movies Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why "Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians" Movies PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War

The theme ran through the three-hour ceremony at the city’s Jordanki Culture Centre, which was regularly interspersed with video messages from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck, each weighing in on AI in entertainment.

Few filmmakers are as closely associated with the debate as Darren Aronofsky , who was honored with Camerimage’s honorary Award for Director . A vocal advocate of generative AI in filmmaking since launching his AI studio Primordial Soup last year , the Requiem for a Dream and Black Swan helmer said it was his third visit to the festival and that he hoped to keep coming back.

“The reason I come back is because there are very rarely film festivals that celebrate the collaboration of everyone,” he said. “They’re very focused on not just the flashy names and that’s really incredible because it honors everyone who makes films possible for people like me.”

Other honorees included Karolina Gruszka, one of Poland’s most acclaimed film and stage actresses, who received the Marshal of the Kujawy Pomorze Region Film Award. Gruszka, who appeared in David Lynch’s last feature, Inland Empire (which was shot in Poland) paid tribute to the late director as a “master investigator” of stories.

Polish cinematographer Janusz Kamiński, longtime Spielberg collaborator and two-time Oscar winner (for Schindler’s List and Saving Private Ryan ) received The Hollywood Reporter ’s Visionary Award for contributions to cinematography. The festival also paid tribute to the late great Polish director Andrzej Wajda ( Man of Iron , Ashes and Diamonds ), a century after his birth and a decade after his death, with a performance by the Polish Radio Choir – Lusławice giving an a cappella reinterpretation of the music from Wajda’s most important films. Poland’s Senate has declared 2026 “The Year of Wajda.”

entertainment.body:
New York rock band The Strokes made their fifth musical guest appearance on Saturday Night Live , performing two songs from their latest studio album, Reality Awaits .

The group, who were last on SNL in 2020 to promote that year’s The New Abnormal , opened with “Lonely in the Future.”

The nine-track album, like its predecessor, was produced by Rick Rubin. In 2022, the band began recording with him in Guanacaste, Costa Rica.

“We rented this house up on the top of a mountain and set the band up outside,” Rubin said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that October. “So they’re playing… It’s like they’re doing a concert for the ocean, on the top of a mountain. It was incredible. And we did that every day, playing out in the [open], and they didn’t want to leave. It was, like, the best experience.”

Guitarist Albert Hammond Jr., who called the album his favorite, described the process: “I don’t think if I told you what it looked like and what it was, you’d fully understand the ‘magical-ness’ of where we were and how it was to record like that.”

Additional recording took place at Rubin’s southern California studios, Shangri-La and The Mansion.

entertainment.summary: The comedian unveils a new impression in his SNL debut
entertainment.body:
Saturday Night Live host, actor and comedian Druski starred in a sketch that imagined a prelude to You Can See Everything , the metadocumentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes .

In the sketch, it is revealed that before the tech fraudster had Nathan Fielder interview her, she talked to Druski. Druski was immediately skeptical of Holmes (Jane Wickline) and her partner, Billy Evans (Ben Marshall).

“Y’all have some of the weirdest, freakiest vibes I’ve ever seen,” he says, before whispering just to the camera: “Whatever they say this bitch did, she done did that s–t.”

Then, during their close-up interview, Druski thinks Holmes is trying to seduce him, so he goes to shut her eyes with his fingers—but they pop right back open.

When Holmes shows Druski a product she is working on, he calls it out: “Okay, listen white girl: I’m gonna say this with all love, right: this is the most Temu-ass piece of s–t I’ve ever seen in my life.”

In the sketch, Druski also uses a technique that Fielder deployed: reenactments.

“I just need to find somebody who can truly embody her character,” he says to himself in the mirror. Cue the cut to him as Holmes.

entertainment.title: Elon Musk Is Portrayed on ‘SNL’: “The Worst Thing South Africa Has Ever Done”
entertainment.summary: Jeremy Culhane plays the character in the show’s latest attempt to assess its relationship with the mogul.
entertainment.body:
Logo text Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars to get humiliated at the polls, but at least he came away with an SNL parody. Jeremy Culhane played the mogul in an appearance with Weekend Update’s Colin Jost as he tried to make sense of his bruising electoral losses. The actor offered a persuasive impression of the mogul’s halting speeches and nonsensical attempts to change the subject with talk of a future that won’t happen. “Imagine,” Culhane’s Musk ended a sentence several times non-sequiturishly. A few days after his major campaign investments came up fruitless (and in a week when his Cybertruck was officially deemed a failure , compounding the injury), comic Musk sought to change the subject “You’re in the news because you wasted half a billion dollars on the midterms… almost all the candidates you backed lost,” Jost said. Related Stories TV Druski Embodies Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything' Spoof on 'SNL' TV James Talarico Crashes 'SNL' Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much

“I’m in the news because my car did a flip… it was like a freaking Hot Wheel,” Musk replied with a Buttheadian enthusiasm. Jost pointed out the irony that “you moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats” and now Texas would be too. “How does that make you feel?” Jost asked. “Bad,” Musk said, before cluelessly changing the topic back to a car flip and barrage of so-you-know-uhs the mogul is known for. (In real life, Musk tried to turn the losses into vindication for the conspiracy theories that he was involved in rigging the 2024 election.) The show’s writers piled on when they had Musk ask Grok to treat him to an “epic vulgar-roast” (Culhane’s coinage for what Musk considers a major burn) and the AI chatbot came back with, “You’re the worst thing South Africa has ever done;” “When you’re on TV it feels like a episode of ‘Hate on the Spectrum’;” and “If you have 100 more kids, maybe one of them will talk to you.” Musk has been in the pop-cultural spotlight this fall with Alex Gibney’s four-hour investigative documentary , which deconstructs the myth of mogul and makes a case he is far more dangerous than caricaturist appearances in Hollywood productions may suggest. Musk has recently has been buying up spectrum, spending $1 billion on Skydance and taking flack for allegedly turning off Starshield and potentially endangering Ukrainian lives. The character had recently been played by Mike Myers, as in a cold open appearance a year ago as he maniacally bellowed “Legalize Comedy” behind portrayals of Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and other appearances in which he did an unhinged air-pounding two-first dance. That impression had a lot of scenery-chewing swings (and more than its share of Mike Myers being Mike Myers), while Culhane Saturday night was more effectively restrained and on-point, leaving the possibility he might be reprising the character on future SNL episodes. Gibney’s film notes how Musk has been savvy at doing cartoonish enough behaviors that people tend to underestimate him, a point that was underscored even in the sketch when, after he went off one more time about a vulgar epic-roast and a car flip, Jost said “I cannot believe you’re the richest person in the world.”
